title: Prioritizing a Multi-Client Assignment (LVN Scope)
subtitle: LVN receives report on 5 clients on a med-surg hall — who is seen first? Applying ABCs, safety, and time-critical needs, then delegating and coordinating the rest
nursesNote: 0700 shift report - The LVN receives report on a 5-client assignment (med-surg hall) and works with one CNA. Room 1 (chart shown): 72 y/o male, COPD with community-acquired pneumonia, day 3; over the last 30 minutes his shortness of breath has increased, oxygen saturation has fallen to 89% on his usual 2 L nasal cannula, he is using accessory muscles, and he appears anxious. Room 2: 84 y/o female, high fall risk (recent hip-fracture history), restless and repeatedly trying to climb out of bed unassisted; the bed alarm is sounding. Room 3: 66 y/o male, type 2 diabetes; scheduled rapid-acting insulin is due now as his breakfast tray arrives. Room 4: 58 y/o female, post-op day 1, requesting pain medication for moderate, stable incisional pain; ordered analgesic is available. Room 5: 70 y/o male, stable and awaiting discharge later today; his family has questions about the discharge paperwork. LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.sub: Which client needs are most urgent
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that represent the MOST urgent client needs on this assignment.

opts.text: Room 1: increasing shortness of breath with oxygen saturation falling to 89% on oxygen and use of accessory muscles
opts.rat: A worsening airway/breathing problem with falling oxygen is the most urgent, life-threatening need (ABC).

opts.text: Room 2: high-fall-risk client restless and repeatedly trying to climb out of bed with the alarm sounding
opts.rat: An imminent fall/injury is a high-priority safety threat requiring prompt intervention.

opts.text: Room 3: scheduled rapid-acting insulin is due now as the breakfast tray arrives
opts.rat: Rapid-acting insulin must be timed with food; it is a time-critical task that cannot be arbitrarily delayed.

opts.text: Room 4: post-op client requesting pain medication for moderate, stable incisional pain
opts.rat: Pain relief is a real need, but stable moderate pain ranks below life-threat, imminent-safety, and time-critical needs.

opts.text: Room 5: family has questions about discharge paperwork
opts.rat: Non-urgent family questions are a low priority that can be acknowledged and addressed after urgent needs.

opts.text: Room 5: client is stable and comfortable awaiting discharge
opts.rat: A stable, comfortable client is a reassuring finding, not an urgent need.

opts.text: Room 4: client's vital signs are stable and within normal limits
opts.rat: Stable vital signs are reassuring and do not indicate an urgent need.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect sound prioritization.

opts.text: Airway and breathing problems take top priority, so Room 1's worsening respiratory distress with falling oxygen is seen first (ABC framework)
opts.rat: Life-threatening airway/breathing needs are the highest priority.

opts.text: After life-threatening needs, imminent safety threats are prioritized, so Room 2's client actively trying to climb out of bed needs prompt intervention
opts.rat: Preventing an imminent fall/injury is the next priority after ABCs.

opts.text: Time-critical medications tied to an event (rapid-acting insulin with a meal) are prioritized over comfort and routine requests, but after life-threat and imminent-safety needs
opts.rat: Event-timed medications are time-critical yet still rank below life-threat and imminent safety.

opts.text: Comfort requests such as pain medication and family questions always come before airway problems
opts.rat: Airway/breathing emergencies outrank comfort and informational requests.

opts.text: Clients should always be seen strictly in room-number order
opts.rat: Room order does not reflect clinical urgency; priority is by acuity and safety.

opts.text: Because the Room 5 client is being discharged, his family's paperwork questions are the top priority
opts.rat: Discharge paperwork is not urgent compared with the acute clinical and safety needs.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.sub: Rank the clients — who is seen first
steps.inst: Drag to rank the clients from FIRST seen (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Room 1 — worsening shortness of breath with oxygen saturation falling to 89%
opts.rat: FIRST — an airway/breathing problem with falling oxygen is the top (life-threat) priority.

opts.text: Room 2 — high-fall-risk client trying to climb out of bed
opts.rat: SECOND — imminent fall/injury is the next priority (safety) after ABCs.

opts.text: Room 3 — scheduled insulin due with the arriving meal tray
opts.rat: THIRD — a time-critical medication tied to the meal, prioritized over comfort and routine needs.

opts.text: Room 4 — post-op client requesting pain medication for moderate pain
opts.rat: FOURTH — a real comfort need, addressed after the acute and time-critical priorities.

opts.text: Room 5 — family with discharge-paperwork questions
opts.rat: LAST — a non-urgent request that is acknowledged and addressed after the priority needs.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Go to Room 1 first, assess breathing and oxygen, position the client upright and ensure oxygen is delivered as ordered, and report the change to the RN
opts.rat: Attending the airway/breathing priority and escalating to the RN is the correct first action.

opts.text: Direct the CNA to stay with and assist the restless fall-risk client in Room 2 and to help with the breakfast trays, while the LVN handles the clinical priorities and retains accountability
opts.rat: Delegating safe, in-scope supervision/assistance to the CNA — while the LVN keeps accountability — helps cover the assignment safely.

opts.text: Coordinate timing so the Room 3 insulin is given with the meal, and keep the team and oncoming staff informed of pending needs
opts.rat: Coordinating time-critical medication with the meal and communicating pending needs maintains safe, continuous care.

opts.text: See all clients strictly in room-number order regardless of urgency
opts.rat: Room order ignores acuity; priority is by clinical urgency and safety.

opts.text: Ask the CNA to assess the Room 1 client's breathing and decide what to do
opts.rat: Assessing and clinically judging a client's breathing is a nursing task, not delegated to a CNA.

opts.text: Ignore the Room 5 family entirely until the end of the shift
opts.rat: Low-priority needs are deferred but still acknowledged; the family is told the LVN will return, not ignored.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: For the Room 1 respiratory client, drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Go to the client, assess airway and breathing and oxygen saturation, and ensure the airway is patent
opts.rat: FIRST — assess airway/breathing and obtain current data.

opts.text: Position the client upright and ensure oxygen is being delivered as ordered
opts.rat: SECOND — within-scope interventions that support breathing immediately.

opts.text: Report the change to the RN using SBAR
opts.rat: THIRD — escalate so the RN can assess and involve the provider.

opts.text: Carry out new orders within scope (e.g., adjust oxygen per order, monitor closely), using read-back for any verbal order
opts.rat: FOURTH — implement ordered interventions correctly and keep monitoring.

opts.text: Document the assessment, interventions, and communication, and coordinate the rest of the assignment by delegating and supervising the CNA
opts.rat: LAST — document and coordinate the remaining assignment so all clients stay safe.

opts.text: After the LVN positioned the Room 1 client upright and ensured oxygen, and the RN assessed and adjusted the plan, the client's oxygen saturation improved and work of breathing eased
opts.rat: Prompt prioritization and escalation improved the client's breathing — the correct outcome.

opts.text: The CNA stayed with and assisted the Room 2 fall-risk client, and no fall occurred
opts.rat: Appropriate delegation kept the at-risk client safe.

opts.text: The Room 3 client received the scheduled insulin timed with the meal
opts.rat: Coordinating the time-critical medication with food was done correctly.

opts.text: The Room 4 client's pain was relieved after the ordered medication was given
opts.rat: The comfort need was met after the higher priorities — an appropriate outcome.

opts.text: The LVN saw clients strictly in room-number order, and the Room 1 client's oxygen fell further before being seen
opts.rat: Ignoring acuity delayed care for the airway priority — a prioritization error to correct.

opts.text: The Room 2 client was left alone and got up unassisted, resulting in a near-fall
opts.rat: Failing to cover the imminent-safety need led to a near-fall — must be corrected.

opts.text: The Room 5 discharge and family questions are still pending, but the family was acknowledged and told the LVN will return
opts.rat: A low-priority need appropriately deferred with acknowledgment — no change and no harm.

opts.text: The Room 4 client's vital signs remain stable and within normal limits
opts.rat: A stable client with no change — expected and requires no new action.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Coordinated Care (the app's 'Management of Care' grouping) — establishing priorities across an assignment — using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Coordinated Care is 18-24% of the NCLEX-PN exam). Concepts reflect standard prioritization frameworks at LVN scope: life-threatening airway/breathing/circulation needs first (ABCs), then imminent safety threats, then time-critical tasks (e.g., rapid-acting insulin timed with a meal), then comfort needs, then routine/informational requests; assessment and clinical judgment stay with the nurse (not delegated to a CNA), while safe, routine, predictable tasks and supervision/assistance may be delegated to a CDPH-certified CNA with the LVN retaining accountability; and changes in condition are escalated to the RN using SBAR. Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation.
